title: For All Souls
theme: Jesus does not want to lose anyone entrusted to Him. Even when we wander away, His invitation remains, and His desire to bring us home does not change.
opening: “And this is the will of the one who sent me, that I should not lose anything of what he gave me, but that I should raise it on the last day.”
prayer: Lord Jesus,  You came to give us eternal life, and You desire that none entrusted to You should be lost.  Today I pray for those who have wandered away from You, especially those who believe they can no longer return. For those who have been hurt, those who have lost faith, and those who no longer recognize Your love, may Your gentle invitation reach their hearts.  Help me to bring others closer to You, not through judgment or fear, but through compassion, patience, and the love You have shown me.  And when I stumble in my own faith, remind me of Your promise that You will not reject anyone who comes to You.  I pray also for all the faithful departed. May Your mercy bring them into the fullness of Your presence, where nothing can separate them from Your love.  Jesus, may none of us lose sight of You, and may we never forget how deeply You desire to bring us home.  Amen.
body:
There is something profoundly comforting in knowing that Jesus does not want to lose us.

In today's Gospel, Jesus speaks of the Father's will, that He should lose nothing of what has been entrusted to Him, but raise it on the last day. These words are not simply a promise of eternal life. They reveal something about the heart of Jesus. He wants us with Him. He wants us to share in the life He has with the Father. And He does not take lightly the possibility of losing even one of us.

Yet later in this same chapter, many of His disciples find His teaching difficult to accept. They turn away and no longer follow Him.

I wonder what Jesus felt as He watched them leave.

I imagine sorrow.

Not anger at having been rejected, or wounded pride because they refused to listen, but sorrow because He knew what they were walking away from. He had offered them the bread of life, the promise of resurrection, a place with Him beyond death. And still, they left.

How often does this happen today?

I think about those who once belonged to the Church but have since walked away. Some may have been hurt. Some may have become disillusioned. Others may have encountered teachings they could not understand or reconcile with their own experiences. And perhaps some simply lost sight of the Jesus they once knew.

I worry about them, not because I believe they are beyond God's reach, but because I wonder whether they realize that the invitation to return is still there.

Jesus says, “I will not reject anyone who comes to me.”

He does not say that we must have followed Him perfectly, that we must never have doubted, or that we must explain every year we spent away. He tells us that whoever comes to Him will not be rejected.

What an extraordinary promise.

And it changes the way I understand my own responsibility to others. If Jesus desires to lose none of those entrusted to Him, shouldn't I also care about those who have wandered away?

Not by judging them, frightening them, or insisting that they believe as I do. But by helping them recognize the Jesus who still welcomes them. Perhaps through a conversation, an act of kindness, an honest acknowledgment of their pain, or simply by loving them without conditions.

I cannot make someone believe. I cannot bring about another person's conversion through my own efforts. But I can help them see that the door they believe has closed may still be open.

And I must remember that this promise is for me, too.

There may be days when my faith feels strong and days when I struggle. There may be times when I misunderstand God, resist His direction, or become so consumed by my own circumstances that I lose sight of Him.

But His desire for me does not begin and end with the strength of my faith.

It begins with His love.

When Jesus turns to the Twelve and asks whether they, too, wish to leave, Peter answers, “Master, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.”

Peter did not understand everything. He would go on to stumble and even deny Jesus. Yet he recognized something worth holding on to: there was nowhere else he could find the life Jesus offered.

On this All Souls' Day, as we remember those who have died and entrust them to God's mercy, I also think of those who are still living but feel far from Him.

I pray they come to know that they have not been forgotten.

Because when Jesus says that the Father's will is for Him to lose nothing entrusted to Him, I hear more than a promise about the last day.

I hear the love of someone who does not want to lose us.

And I hear an invitation that is still being offered.
